query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: High configurational entropy in alloy nanoparticles creates a more uniform atomic bonding environment and a distributed lattice strain at the surface, which together increase the local cohesion and delay the onset of surface premelting, thereby raising the bulk melting temperature compared to lower‐complexity (binary or ternary) nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized as homogeneous high-entropy alloys with a random, near-equimolar distribution of multiple metal elements, having similar size (e.g., 5–50 nm) and spherical morphology.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles with equivalent sizes and morphologies: one set with high configurational entropy (multicomponent, ≥5 elements) and a control set with lower configurational entropy (binary or ternary alloys) under otherwise identical synthesis conditions.
generation.conditions: Subject both sets to a controlled thermal ramp under an inert atmosphere (e.g., using differential scanning calorimetry and in situ high-resolution TEM) ensuring identical heating rates, to monitor surface disordering (premelting) and bulk melting behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform atomic-scale distribution of different elements and the associated homogeneous lattice strain at the nanoparticle surfaces.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy promotes a uniform distribution of interatomic interactions that minimizes local energy imbalances at the surface. This uniformity and distributed strain increase the cohesive energy barriers to atomic disordering, thereby delaying the formation of a premelted surface layer. In contrast, lower-complexity nanoparticles exhibit localized compositional heterogeneities that act as nucleation sites for early surface premelting.
generation.predicted_outcome: High-entropy nanoparticles will show a statistically significant delay in the onset of surface premelting and an increase in the bulk melting temperature relative to the binary or ternary control nanoparticles under the same heating conditions.
generation.baseline: Lower-entropy nanoparticles (e.g., binary or ternary alloys) synthesized with equivalent size and morphology, which are expected to exhibit an earlier onset of surface disordering and a lower bulk melting temperature.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for nanoparticles within the 5–50 nm size range and under inert or controlled atmospheres where extrinsic effects (like oxidation) are minimized. The behavior may differ if particle sizes become very large or if surface modifications dominate the thermal response.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative delay in premelting is expected, the precise magnitude of the shift in onset temperature between high-entropy and lower-entropy nanoparticles is not predetermined and may depend on specific elemental combinations and processing details.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of nanoparticles with identical sizes and shapes: one group being high-entropy (≥5 elements) and the other a simpler binary/ternary control. Subject both groups to the same controlled thermal ramp in an inert environment while monitoring their structural evolution using DSC and in situ TEM. Quantitatively record the onset temperature for surface disordering (premelting) and the full melting transition.
measurements: DSC thermograms to determine the onset temperature of premelting and bulk melting peaks
High-resolution TEM images to detect the progression of surface disordering
Surface composition analyses to verify homogeneous mixing in high-entropy nanoparticles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy nanoparticles do not exhibit a statistically significant delay in the onset of surface premelting and do not demonstrate a higher bulk melting temperature compared to the control nanoparticles under identical experimental conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of five or more principal elements with a near equimolar ratio, have become one of the most transformative concepts in current alloy design. Homogenous mixing of a large number of elements induces synergistic effects among different elements, thus resulting in an unusual combination of functional properties appealing to a broad range of applications such as structural alloys, catalysis, sensing, and energy storage. While the synthesis of bulk HEAs has been the main focus in the past decade, nano-sized HEA particles are emerging as a new class of multifunctional materials due to their more fascinating properties. Scalable and economically viable synthetic methods for HEA nanoparticles (NPs) are of particular interest, yet the controlled incorporation of multiple elements into a tiny particle (<100 nm) remains a significant challenge. In 2018, a carbothermal shock (CTS) technique was developed to incorporate multiple immiscible metal elements into a single NP and successfully demonstrated the synthesis of HEA NPs containing up to eight elements uniformly dispersed on a conductive carbon support. High-entropy alloys, containing five or even more metals, have attracted significant attentions, because of their unique chemical and physical complexity, which endow alloys with tunable features and properties such as thermal stability, superior corrosion resistance, high hardness, exceptional ductility, and superparamagnetism. A wide range of researches have revealed that the nanoparticles loading on the supports could significantly improve specific surface area and surface energy compared with the bulk materials or the nanoparticles themselves,. In addition, in industrial applications, the nanoparticles need to be dispersedly immobilized on granular supports, such as Al2O3, zeolite, and carbon materials etc., which can make the catalysts feature with tunable size, shape, and stability, enhancing the catalytic performance. Therefore, the supported high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) can be promisingly applied in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles. drafts.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by the interplay between high configurational entropy (which homogenizes interatomic interactions throughout the nanoparticle) and the differential surface energies of the constituent elements. Higher configurational entropy enhances overall thermal stability by delaying the onset of surface premelting and increasing the bulk melting temperature compared to lower-entropy systems.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized as high-entropy alloys in a spherical morphology with a random distribution of multiple metallic elements, produced under uniform synthesis conditions.
drafts.intervention: Systematically vary the alloy composition to adjust configurational entropy while keeping particle size, morphology, and synthesis parameters constant.
drafts.conditions: Nanoparticles should be measured under controlled inert ambient conditions over a defined temperature ramp (using techniques like differential scanning calorimetry) and imaged with high-resolution transmission electron microscopy to capture surface and bulk changes; comparisons are made between high-entropy (high configurational entropy) and lower-entropy (e.g., binary or ternary alloy) nanoparticles.
drafts.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale distribution of different elements, especially at the near-surface region where differences in surface energy become critical, mediates the melting behavior.
drafts.mechanism: The high configurational entropy leads to a more uniform and energetically favorable distribution of bonding interactions, which enhances the cohesive energy of the nanoparticle. This stabilization retards surface premelting by reducing the local energy imbalances that would otherwise promote early disordering. Additionally, differences in surface energies among the constituent metals create localized sites of preferential disordering that, in lower-entropy systems, coalesce more readily into a premelted phase.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with higher configurational entropy are predicted to exhibit a higher bulk melting temperature and a delayed or reduced premelting regime. In contrast, nanoparticles with lower configurational entropy will initiate premelting at lower temperatures, showing more pronounced surface disordering before complete melting.
drafts.baseline: The baseline for comparison is provided by nanoparticles composed of single metals or low-entropy (e.g., binary/ternary) alloys where conventional melting behavior (earlier onset of premelting and lower melting temperature) is observed.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold over the nanoparticle size range (approximately 5–50 nm) and under thermal conditions that do not introduce extrinsic factors such as oxidation or extreme pressure. It may be less applicable if other surface modification processes dominate or if particle size effects become overwhelming.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles that systematically vary in configurational entropy by adjusting the proportion of multiple metallic elements, while ensuring identical size and morphology. Characterize their thermal behavior using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the onset of premelting and melting temperature and employ high-resolution TEM to image surface disorder. Complement with surface-sensitive techniques (e.g., XPS) to verify the uniformity of elemental distribution.
measurements: DSC thermograms showing onset temperatures for premelting and complete melting
HR-TEM images capturing the initiation and progression of surface premelting
XPS or similar data confirming surface composition uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with higher configurational entropy do not show a statistically significant increase in melting temperature or a delayed onset of premelting compared to lower-entropy systems under otherwise identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Premelting and melting in high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by the extent of surface segregation of low melting point elements. In nanoparticles with a uniform elemental distribution, any local enrichment at surfaces of one or more constituents with lower cohesive energies reduces the local melting barrier, triggering premelting that spreads inward. Thus, controlling surface segregation determines the onset and progression of melting.
drafts.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized with near-equimolar bulk composition and a uniform surface distribution of elements.
drafts.intervention: Induce controlled surface segregation via a post‐synthesis thermal treatment (or quenching protocol) to selectively enrich the nanoparticle surface with a lower melting point constituent.
drafts.conditions: Nanoparticles of similar size (e.g., below ~50 nm) and shape, prepared in two groups: one with unaltered (uniform) surface composition and one subjected to surface segregation treatment, heated under identical conditions with controlled ramp rates under inert atmosphere.
drafts.structural_mediator: Surface composition gradient, in which the low melting point element is enriched at the nanoparticle surface.
drafts.mechanism: Surface enrichment decreases local cohesive energy at the particle interfaces, lowering the energy barrier for atomic mobility; this leads to early melting of the surface (premelting) that increasingly destabilizes the core structure as the temperature rises.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that have undergone induced surface segregation (and thus have enriched low melting point elements at their surfaces) will display a measurable decrease in the temperature at which premelting and bulk melting initiate compared to the baseline with uniformly distributed elements.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles without artificial enhancement of surface segregation, where the melting behavior reflects the average cohesive energy derived from the equimolar composition.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate for particle sizes where surface effects are significant (e.g., nanoparticles below ~50 nm) and for compositions in which at least one component has a notably lower melting point than the others. Its influence may diminish in larger particles where bulk properties prevail.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles with identical overall composition and size distributions. Subject one set to a thermal treatment known to promote surface segregation (enriching the surface in the identified low melting point element) and leave the other set untreated. Then, heat both sets under identical conditions using a controlled temperature ramp while monitoring the onset of premelting and complete melting.
measurements: Temperature at which premelting initiates (via in situ TEM or high-resolution calorimetric methods)
Temperature at which complete melting occurs (via differential scanning calorimetry)
Surface composition analysis (using XPS or EDS) to confirm the extent of segregation
Morphological changes in the nanoparticles observed by TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with induced surface segregation do not show a statistically significant reduction in the onset temperatures for premelting and complete melting (relative to the uniformly composed nanoparticles), the hypothesis that surface segregation governs the melting behavior in these nanoparticles would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of supported high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by localized lattice strain generated by atomic size mismatches and high configurational entropy, which together produce heterogeneous bond strengths that stabilize the nanoparticle surfaces against early melting.
drafts.material_initial_state: Supported high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., single‐phase HEA such as TiZrHfMoNb) that are uniformly alloyed in a solid solution state.
drafts.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles with similar average sizes and supports: one set with high configurational entropy (≥5 elements) and a control set with lower configurational complexity (e.g., binary or trinary alloys).
drafts.conditions: Subject both sets to a controlled thermal ramp (e.g., from room temperature to above the expected melting point) under inert or controlled atmosphere, ensuring identical heating rates and environmental conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice strain and atomic-level heterogeneity at the nanoparticle surfaces arising from a high degree of atomic mixing.
drafts.mechanism: High configurational entropy enforces a uniform dispersion of lattice strain that increases the energy barrier for surface atomic diffusion. This effect delays the onset of surface premelting and modifies the melting progression relative to lower-entropy systems where atomic segregation (or less strain-tolerant bonding) facilitates earlier local melting.
drafts.predicted_outcome: High-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit a statistically significant delay in the onset temperature of premelting and a more gradual melting transition compared to lower-entropy nanoparticles of similar size and support.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles with lower configurational entropy (e.g., binary or trinary alloys) synthesized under identical conditions.
drafts.boundary: This phenomenon is expected to hold for nanoparticles below ~100 nm over a temperature range spanning from the onset of surface premelting (potentially several tens to a few hundred degrees below full melting) up to complete melting, with effects potentially moderated by the interaction with the support.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles with identical sizes and supported substrates: one set consisting of high-entropy (≥5 elements) alloys and a control set with a simpler binary or trinary composition. Conduct identical in situ heating experiments (using techniques such as TEM and DSC) while gradually increasing the temperature in an inert atmosphere.
measurements: Onset temperature of surface premelting (as observed via in situ imaging)
Full melting temperature from calorimetric data
Rate of change in nanoparticle morphology during heating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant delay in the onset of premelting or alteration in the melting profile is observed in high-entropy nanoparticles compared to the lower-entropy controls under identical experimental conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior in high‐entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles is governed by the atomic-scale heterogeneity induced by configurational entropy and lattice strain from atomic size mismatches. This heterogeneity creates localized surface sites with lower cohesive energies that serve as nucleation points for premelting, thereby controlling the onset and progression of melting.
drafts.material_initial_state: Monodisperse HEA nanoparticles (composed of five or more near-equimolar elements with significant atomic size dispersion) that are uniformly dispersed, for example, on an inert granular support.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled temperature ramp via in situ heating (e.g., in a high-resolution TEM or using differential scanning calorimetry) to monitor the nanoparticle structure from below the premelting onset through complete melting.
drafts.conditions: Tests over the temperature interval ranging from a point well below the anticipated premelting onset to above the bulk melting point, with a parallel controlled comparison using monometallic or binary nanoparticles (of similar size) under identical thermal conditions, and with/without support confinement.
drafts.structural_mediator: Localized surface heterogeneities such as low-coordination atoms and strained regions arising from the random mixing of differing element sizes and bonding strengths.
drafts.mechanism: The high configurational entropy in HEAs produces a wide distribution of local bond strengths and lattice distortions. These areas of low cohesive energy at the nanoparticle surfaces lower the energy barrier for atomic disordering, initiating premelting at lower temperatures than the bulk melting point. In addition, support interactions (or lack thereof) can moderate surface diffusion and affect the extent of premelting.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to monometallic or simpler alloy counterparts, HEA nanoparticles are expected to show an earlier and more gradual onset of surface disordering (premelting) while retaining a high overall stability or bulk melting temperature. Moreover, immobilized nanoparticles on inert supports should exhibit suppressed or delayed premelting relative to free-standing ones.
drafts.baseline: Monometallic or binary nanoparticles of comparable size that exhibit sharper melting transitions with minimal early surface premelting.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for nanoparticles roughly <100 nm in diameter and for HEA compositions meeting design criteria (e.g., atomic size differences >5% and moderate negative enthalpies of mixing). Extreme variations in size or compositions outside this regime might not follow the same behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) heating experiments on size-controlled HEA nanoparticles and on matched monometallic nanoparticles, both free-standing and immobilized on inert supports. Record the onset temperature for observable surface disorder (premelting) and the complete melting transition using complementary differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).
measurements: TEM imaging to monitor surface disorder and morphological changes
DSC to detect endothermic peaks corresponding to premelting and melting
Surface-sensitive spectroscopy (e.g., XPS) to assess changes in atomic coordination
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HEA nanoparticles do not exhibit a statistically significant lower temperature onset of surface disorder (premelting) relative to the baseline monometallic/binary nanoparticles, or if no correlation is observed between the degree of lattice strain heterogeneity and the onset/manner of melting, then the hypothesis is falsified.
